name: Ogma
summary: NASA tool that turns formal requirements (FRET output, diagrams, temporal-logic specs) into runtime monitors and the glue code to run them inside ROS 2 nodes, Core Flight System apps or F Prime components. The monitors themselves are generated by Copilot as hard real-time C99.
why_it_matters: The shortest open path from 'the nav solution must never do X' to a running safety monitor next to your algorithm. That monitor is the piece a runtime-assurance argument is built on.
hackathon_notes: Needs a Haskell toolchain (GHC + cabal) to build, which is the main setup cost. Write 3-5 properties (innovation gate, max position jump, staleness of the nav message) and generate a ROS 2 monitor node that subscribes to your estimate. Good slide material even if only run in SITL.

name: Copilot
summary: Stream-based runtime-verification language embedded in Haskell. It compiles monitors to constant-time, constant-memory C99 (and Bluespec), so the generated checker can run on a flight controller-class MCU.
why_it_matters: Bounded-time, no-heap C output is what an embedded safety monitor needs. It is the engine behind Ogma.
hackathon_notes: GitHub reports no license; the copilot/LICENSE file in the repo is BSD-3 text. Use through Ogma unless the team already knows Haskell. The generated C can be dropped into a PX4 module or a companion process.

name: R2U2
summary: Runtime monitor framework for Mission-time Linear Temporal Logic. A compiler (C2PO) turns specs into a compact binary that a small C or Rust engine evaluates on streaming sensor data, sized for constrained flight hardware.
why_it_matters: Temporal properties such as 'innovation above gate for more than 2 s implies fallback' are exactly what a nav health monitor checks. R2U2 evaluates them on a microcontroller budget.
hackathon_notes: Python 3.9+ for the spec compiler, a C99 compiler for the engine. Replay a ulog or bag through it offline to show which seconds of a flight the monitor would have flagged. Small project (tens of stars), so expect thin docs.

name: FRET
summary: NASA's Formal Requirements Elicitation Tool: write requirements in a structured English (FRETish), get temporal-logic formalisations, consistency checks and test cases. Exports feed Ogma and other monitor generators.
why_it_matters: Certification work starts from requirements. Writing the nav function's safety requirements in FRET gives a traceable artifact that maps to the DO-178C requirements-based mindset.
hackathon_notes: Electron desktop app. License is a NASA agreement in LICENSE.pdf (GitHub reports NOASSERTION; not read here). A 30-minute exercise: 5 requirements for the nav output, exported to Ogma, shown as one slide of traceability.

name: run-time-assurance (AFRL ACT3)
summary: Python library of runtime-assurance safety filters from the AFRL ACT3 team: generic explicit and implicit Simplex plus explicit and implicit ASIF (active set invariance filter), with a zoo of worked examples. Constraints and a state-transition model are all a new module needs.
why_it_matters: One of very few public, code-level RTA implementations from a defense lab. It shows the switch logic and constraint style a reviewer will expect when you claim 'simplex architecture'.
hackathon_notes: LICENSE says only 'This software is government owned'; the README carries an AFRL public-release case number. Fine to read and learn from; ask before shipping it. Examples target spacecraft docking, so adapt the constraint set to nav (position bound, innovation bound).

name: SOTER on ROS
summary: Research framework that builds distributed mobile-robot software on ROS as runtime-assurance modules: an advanced controller, a safe controller and a decision module that switches between them. Written in the P language (generated C#) with C++ robot modules.
why_it_matters: A worked ROS example of the simplex switch with a formal decision module. Useful as a pattern reference, not as a dependency.
hackathon_notes: Last push 2020-06, ROS 1, no license file. Read for the architecture only; reimplement the switch in your own node.

name: F Prime (F')
summary: JPL's component-based flight software framework: typed ports, a modelling language (FPP) and generated C++ glue, flown on the Mars Helicopter. Runs on Linux, RTOSes and microcontrollers.
why_it_matters: Shows what flight-grade structure looks like (static allocation, explicit interfaces, telemetry/command dictionaries). A nav module written as an F' component is easier to argue about than a ROS node.
hackathon_notes: Too heavy to adopt in 48 h. Cite it on the path-to-product slide as the target structure, and borrow its patterns (no dynamic allocation after init, rate groups).

name: NASA Core Flight System (cFS)
summary: NASA Goddard's reusable flight software framework: a publish/subscribe software bus, an OS abstraction layer and a library of flight apps. Used on many spacecraft and some UAS research programmes.
why_it_matters: The other mainstream flight-software reference architecture. Ogma generates monitors directly as cFS apps.
hackathon_notes: Reference only for a hackathon. Builds on Linux in under an hour if you need to demo an Ogma monitor in its native host.

name: ros2_tracing
summary: LTTng-based instrumentation for ROS 2: tracepoints in rclcpp/rcl/rmw plus tools to record and analyse callback durations and message flow end to end.
why_it_matters: The way to measure, not guess, the camera-to-setpoint latency of a ROS 2 nav pipeline. That number goes straight into EKF2_EV_DELAY / VISO_DELAY_MS and onto the latency-budget slide.
hackathon_notes: Linux only (LTTng kernel/userspace packages). Trace a 60 s replay, then report p50/p99 callback latency per node. Pairs with tracetools_analysis notebooks.

name: ROS 2 reference-system
summary: ROS 2 Real-Time Working Group benchmark that simulates an autonomous-driving node graph to compare executors, middleware and OS settings on latency and dropped messages.
why_it_matters: Gives a defensible method for choosing executor and middleware settings on a companion computer instead of defaults.
hackathon_notes: Last push 2023-09. Use the method, not the code: copy the measurement approach onto your own graph.

name: ROS 2 real-time examples
summary: Minimal recipes for real-time ROS 2: memory locking, thread priorities, CPU pinning and callback-group separation.
why_it_matters: Short, copyable patterns for keeping the nav callback off the same thread as logging and image I/O.
hackathon_notes: Last push 2024-01. Apply two recipes (mlockall, SCHED_FIFO on the estimator thread) and show the latency histogram before and after.

name: TensorRT (open-source components)
summary: Open parts of NVIDIA's inference SDK: parsers, plugins, samples and the trtexec / Polygraphy tools for building and profiling engines from ONNX.
why_it_matters: On a Jetson this is how a matcher or VPR backbone gets from 'works in PyTorch' to a fixed, measurable latency. trtexec timings are the numbers to quote.
hackathon_notes: JetPack already ships TensorRT; this repo is for samples and Polygraphy. Export ONNX, run `trtexec --onnx=model.onnx --fp16`, record mean and p99 latency. Engines are tied to the GPU and TensorRT version: rebuild on the target.

name: AIMET (AI Model Efficiency Toolkit)
summary: Qualcomm's quantization and compression library for PyTorch and ONNX models: post-training quantization, quantization-aware training and accuracy debugging, aimed at INT8 deployment on Snapdragon NPUs.
why_it_matters: Qualcomm flight boards (RB5, VOXL 2) need INT8 models for the NPU. AIMET is the vendor path to get there without large accuracy loss.
hackathon_notes: Repo moved from quic/aimet to qualcomm/aimet. License file is BSD-3-style (GitHub reports NOASSERTION). Only worth the setup if the team has a Qualcomm board in hand.

name: Qualcomm AI Hub Models
summary: Collection of models exported for Qualcomm devices, each with a perf.yaml of measured on-device latency and memory per runtime (TFLite, QNN, ONNX) and precision. Includes SuperPoint (the MIT rpautrat version), ResNet, depth models and more.
why_it_matters: Published per-device latency for nav-relevant networks on Qualcomm silicon, including the RB3 Gen 2 robotics kit. It is the cheapest source of a cited NPU number.
hackathon_notes: Read src/qai_hub_models/models/<model>/perf.yaml for numbers. No QRB5165 (RB5 / VOXL 2) entry as of 2026-11-09; the closest robotics board is the RB3 Gen 2 Vision Kit. Profiling on hosted devices needs a free Qualcomm account.

name: Jetson Benchmarks
summary: NVIDIA scripts that reproduce its published Jetson inference benchmarks with TensorRT on a set of reference networks.
why_it_matters: Lets a team reproduce vendor numbers on their own board and power mode before quoting them.
hackathon_notes: Last push 2024-06; covers Nano / Xavier generations more than Orin. Treat its numbers as vendor claims.

name: Isaac ROS Benchmark
summary: ros2_benchmark-based scripts NVIDIA uses to produce the Isaac ROS performance tables (throughput and latency per node or graph per Jetson / dGPU platform).
why_it_matters: Source of the cited Orin Nano Super numbers for stereo disparity and AprilTag; the same harness can measure your own node at a fixed input rate.
hackathon_notes: Needs the Isaac ROS dev container. Useful for 'measured at 30 Hz input' latency the same way NVIDIA reports it.

name: ncnn
summary: Dependency-free C++ inference engine tuned for ARM CPUs (NEON) with optional Vulkan GPU. Its benchmark/README.md lists per-board latency for a fixed model set, including Raspberry Pi 5 and Jetson AGX Orin.
why_it_matters: The practical CPU-only inference path on a Raspberry Pi 5 or other ARM companion, and a published per-board baseline to compare against.
hackathon_notes: BSD-3 for ncnn itself, with third-party components under their own terms (LICENSE.txt). Run `benchncnn` on your board to reproduce the README numbers before porting your own model via pnnx.

name: jetson-stats (jtop)
summary: Monitoring tool for NVIDIA Jetson: CPU/GPU load, clocks, temperatures, power rails and power mode, with a Python API for logging.
why_it_matters: The easy way to put a measured watts number next to a latency number, which is what an onboard-compute slide needs.
hackathon_notes: AGPL-3.0: fine as a dev tool on the bench, do not bundle it into a shipped image. `sudo pip3 install jetson-stats` on the Jetson itself (ask before installing).

name: VersaVIS
summary: Open hardware and firmware board that hardware-triggers multiple cameras and an IMU and timestamps them on one clock, with ROS drivers. Designed for visual-inertial rigs.
why_it_matters: Shows the hardware-sync approach (trigger plus exposure-time compensation) that removes most camera-IMU timing error before any software sync is needed.
hackathon_notes: Last push 2021-09, ROS 1. License file is BSD-3 text (GitHub reports NOASSERTION). Cite the design; for a hackathon, use a camera with a hardware trigger input wired to an FC camera-trigger output instead.

name: alpha-beta-CROWN
summary: GPU-accelerated neural-network verifier that proves bounds on a network's outputs over a set of inputs. Winner of the VNN-COMP verification competition several years running (per its README).
why_it_matters: One concrete answer to 'how would you assure the learned part': prove a small learned component (for example a confidence head) stays bounded over a stated input envelope.
hackathon_notes: Scales to small and medium networks, not to a full ViT backbone. BSD-3-style license file (GitHub reports NOASSERTION). Mention on the assurance slide; do not try to verify a feature matcher in 48 h.
